title: Capacity Columns
context: Grade 4, the chapter's closing topic, where the column work is done a third time and then put to use. An adult sees the weight columns again with new units. What is actually being taught is the question's own words. Example 17 asks how much water is left and ends by calling its answer the difference. Exercise 11.6 asks who sold more and how much more. The Critical Thinking box uses petrol, buys more and uses again, and in its second week the petrol has to be bought before it is used. Otherwise the tank would go below empty. The Math Lab prints its results for the one litre bottle before anyone pours, and this tool shows no count until the pouring is done. Apply Your Skills asks three questions about facts the chapter does not give; this tool answers none of them.

writeup.why: Add and take away capacities in litres and millilitres, answer what the question asks in its own words, and count the jars that fill a bottle.
writeup.look: A tank at the left, a litres and millilitres frame in the middle, and a jar shelf with two bottles and an empty results table at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Capacity Columns' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns worked or the story's lines run against what this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column's answer lands or each line of the story runs on the tank, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the fourth phase it counts the pourings made with the jar in hand and shows no second number, because how many pourings fill the bottle is the thing being found. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tank stands at the left of the working area, 200 by 300 at 64,214, marked up its side in litres, its pale blue water level drawn to that scale. The story card sits under it, 200 by 120 at 64,526, listing the amounts used and added in the order the story gives, one to a line, and the run control under that, 200 by 44 at 64,660, plays the story one line at a time, the level falling for each amount used and rising for each amount added. A line that would take the level below the tank's floor stops it at the floor, and what could not be taken hangs under the floor as a dashed outline. The unit switch runs across the middle, 460 by 44 at 290,214, reading L and mL, km and m, or kg and g. The column frame stands under it, 460 by 300 at 290,270: the larger unit's column at the left, the smaller unit's at the right cut into exactly three digit boxes under all three settings, a near-black line between them, and the joining sign over the smaller column reading a thousand. Up to three rows, a rule, and the answer row. Adding works the smaller column first, and each full thousand of it gathers into one deep blue chip of the larger unit that rises over the larger column, while what is left goes down as three digits. Taking away starts at the smaller column too. When the millilitres on top are fewer than those below, or read zero zero zero, the column stays shut and the break control, 220 by 44 at 290,584, lights over the litres on top: it strikes them through, writes one less above in amber, and pours one litre across the line as a thousand millilitres into the millilitres on top, which are rewritten a thousand more above them in amber. The answer card sits under the frame, 460 by 90 at 290,640, a blank with the question's own words printed round it: water left in the tank, which is more and by how much, or the total. At the right the jar shelf stands, 380 by 250 at 770,214: jars of one hundred, two hundred, two hundred and fifty and five hundred millilitres in a row with a bucket of water, and a one litre and a two litre bottle beside them; an item may set its own glass, mug or jug at the shelf's end in place of the jars. A jar dipped in the bucket fills to its brim, and tipped over a bottle it pours until it is empty or the bottle is full to its neck line, whichever comes first; a jar that stops pouring with water still in it keeps that water drawn in it. Each pouring is one sky blue mark on the pour counter, 380 by 44 at 770,634. The results table stands between them, 380 by 140 at 770,480, a row for each bottle and a column for each jar, and when a bottle reaches its neck line the counter's marks are counted and only then drop into their cell. Every cell starts empty. The sort rail folds out over the results table in free play and lines up measures written in one unit, such as throws turned into centimetres, from largest to smallest. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across and has no dot key. On the first two phases the answer slot is a two-part measure with three boxes for the smaller unit. On the third the answer card's words are chosen from keys printed with the question's own phrases, and a measure typed before the words are chosen waits beside the card. On the fourth the slot takes a count, with the word pourings printed beside it. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green: metres beside kilometres, centimetres beside metres, millimetres, grams and millilitres. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that fills an empty place of the smaller unit is grey. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape, and the mark where a reading is taken, are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket, strike line, table rule and panel edge, is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, and a count by the slot that names what is counted, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in the smaller unit's places is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A figure that goes down by one when a unit is broken is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. No measure in two units is written as a decimal anywhere on the stage. No jar count is written anywhere on this stage until its own pouring has been done, not in the table, not on the shelf and not in a caption, so the counts the children find are their own. The broken litre is drawn as a thousand millilitres pouring across the line, and never as so many smaller jars. The tank plays a story in its card's order unless the child sets another order on purpose.
writeup.finish: The card shows the tank at its last level with its answer card, the last sum or difference in the frame, and the results table with the counts the child poured.

phases.win: both rows stand with every millilitres box filled, and the three boxes stay under grams and metres too
phases.does: types each capacity into the frame, filling every millilitres box, then flips the unit switch to see the same three boxes for grams and metres
phases.goal: beside litres, millilitres take three places, as grams and metres do
phases.says: The millilitres column has three boxes. How is a two-digit number of millilitres written?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write 9 L 6 mL in columns. Then write 9 kg 6 g. What changes in the smaller column?
phases.feels: a thousand joins each of these pairs, so the smaller unit keeps three boxes under every heading here
phases.hands: Draw two columns on the board headed L and mL, with three boxes under the mL. Write 23 L 400 mL, then ask the class to write 16 L 57 mL under it, and fill the hundreds box with a zero. Then relabel the columns kg and g, and then km and m, and ask whether the three boxes change.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many millilitres boxes are there? Second rung, the phase's: which places does this number fill? Third rung: the card is cut to a single-digit number of millilitres, and the child fills all three boxes before the longer card comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: digits are written from the left, and the first box is where writing begins.
wrong.move: types the fifty-seven millilitres into the first two millilitres boxes, so the row reads five hundred and seventy millilitres.
wrong.screen: the row is read back aloud as it stands, five hundred and seventy millilitres, and a jug beside it is filled to that line, over half a litre, beside the card's own small measure. The five and the seven slide one box to the right, and a grey zero drops into the hundreds box at full size. The child's row stays drawn above the new one, nothing marked.

wrong.why: an earlier frame, metres and centimetres, had two boxes on its smaller side, and that is the frame remembered with metres.
wrong.move: after switching to kilometres and metres, types twelve kilometres seventy-five metres with the seventy-five in two boxes, as if the metres were centimetres beside metres.
wrong.screen: the metres column keeps its three boxes under the new heading, and the seven and the five slide into the tens and the ones with a grey zero in the hundreds. The joining sign reads a thousand, the same as for litres, and the child's row stays drawn above the new one.

phases.screen: the frame with two capacities waiting, one with a two-digit number of millilitres
phases.soWhat: Beside litres the millilitres take three places, as grams do beside kilograms and metres beside kilometres.

phases.win: the carried litre rides over the litres column, and the broken litre spreads into a thousand millilitres
phases.does: carries a litre in the sum, then breaks a litre in the difference
phases.goal: a thousand millilitres are carried as one litre, and a litre is broken into a thousand millilitres to borrow
phases.says: More than a thousand here, too few there. Carry a litre, or break one?
phases.check: Add 15 L 650 mL and 7 L 480 mL. Then take 9 L 875 mL from 20 L 300 mL.
phases.feels: a litre is a thousand millilitres whichever way it travels, into the litres or out of them
phases.hands: Write 12 L 760 mL and 9 L 580 mL in columns and add the millilitres first: one thousand three hundred and forty. Carry one litre and write three hundred and forty. Then write 25 L 200 mL less 8 L 650 mL: the millilitres on top are too few, so break one litre into a thousand millilitres. Ask which way the litre travelled each time.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is this a sum or a take-away? Second rung, the phase's: is a litre carried, or broken? Third rung: the frame is cut to amounts just over or just under a thousand millilitres, and the child carries or breaks before the larger amounts come back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the millilitres sum is one number, and splitting a number that has just been made feels wrong.
wrong.move: writes all of one thousand two hundred and fifteen in the millilitres column, and gets forty-five litres and a four-digit number of millilitres.
wrong.screen: the millilitres sum shows one thousand two hundred and fifteen, and a thousand of those millilitres gather into one deep blue litre chip that rises over the litres, leaving two hundred and fifteen below. The child's four digits are laid over the three boxes and the first has no box to stand in. The litres are added again with the chip, forty-six, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a metre breaks into a hundred centimetres, and litre sounds like metre.
wrong.move: breaks a litre into a hundred millilitres, as a metre breaks into centimetres, and finds two hundred and twenty millilitres on top, still too few to take four hundred and eighty.
wrong.screen: the joining sign lights, a thousand, and the broken litre pours across the line as a thousand millilitres, the millilitres on top rewritten above them in amber as one thousand one hundred and twenty. Four hundred and eighty are then taken, leaving six hundred and forty, and the litres, thirty-three less sixteen, make seventeen. The child's working stays drawn beside it.

wrong.why: taking the smaller number from the larger is the only take-away that seems to work, whichever line each stands on.
wrong.move: takes the smaller millilitres from the larger, four hundred and eighty less a hundred and twenty, and writes eighteen litres three hundred and sixty millilitres.
wrong.screen: the millilitres column stays shut on the hundred and twenty on top, and the child's three hundred and sixty is written small beside it. The break control strikes through thirty-four, writes thirty-three above it in amber, and a thousand millilitres join the hundred and twenty. The take-away runs, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a sum whose millilitres come to more than a thousand, and a difference with too few millilitres on top
phases.soWhat: Each full thousand millilitres is carried as one litre. To borrow, break one litre into a thousand millilitres, and the litres on top go down by one.

phases.win: the tank settles at its level, and the answer card reads the amount left in the tank
phases.does: runs the story on the tank, works the difference in the frame, and writes the answer as what is left
phases.goal: the answer says what the question asks, such as how much is left, not just a difference
phases.says: What does the question ask for? Say the answer in those words.
phases.check: A drum has 30 L of water. 12 L 750 mL is used, then 8 L is added. How much water is in the drum now?
phases.feels: the tank keeps the story's order, and only its last level answers the question
phases.hands: Fill a bucket to a marked line and tell a story aloud, pouring as you go: some water used for plants, some added from a jug, some used again. After each step ask the class where the level is now. At the end ask what the question wants, the water left, and let a child say the answer in those words.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the question ask for? Second rung, the phase's: which line of the story comes first? Third rung: the story is cut to one use and one addition, and the child runs it on the tank before the longer story comes back. The answer card's words and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: the first take-away gave a neat answer to a question about what is left, and it feels like the end.
wrong.move: stops after the first line of the story and answers twenty-one litres four hundred millilitres, the water left after the first use.
wrong.screen: the tank plays on from where the child stopped: twelve litres go in and the level rises, twenty-five litres three hundred and fifty millilitres go out and it falls, and it settles at eight litres fifty millilitres. The run control lights each line of the story card in turn, and the child's answer stays on the card beside the tank's last level.

wrong.why: the two amounts used seem to belong together, and the order of the story's lines is easy to pass over.
wrong.move: takes the second amount used before adding the twelve litres, finds it more than the twenty-one litres four hundred millilitres in the tank, takes the smaller from the larger, and ends on fifteen litres nine hundred and fifty millilitres.
wrong.screen: the tank plays the child's order: the level falls to the floor and stops there, and three litres nine hundred and fifty millilitres that could not be taken hang under the floor as a dashed outline. The story then runs in its card's order, the twelve litres going in first, and the level settles at eight litres fifty millilitres, the child's answer staying on the card.

wrong.why: the working ends on a number, and the last number written feels like the answer.
wrong.move: types eight litres fifty millilitres with no words chosen, leaving a bare difference as the answer.
wrong.screen: the measure waits beside the answer card, and the card's words, water left in the tank, light around the blank. The tank's last level is lit in reddish purple beside it, and once the words are set, the measure drops into the blank.

phases.screen: the tank full to a mark, a story card, and the answer card with its blank reading how much is left
phases.soWhat: Work a story's steps in the order it gives. Answer in the question's own words: what is left, not just a difference.

phases.win: the bottle fills, the count drops into its cell, and the next jar waits with its cell still empty
phases.does: chooses a jar, fills and pours it until the bottle is full, counting each pouring, and writes the count in the table
phases.goal: a jar fills a bottle in a number of pourings, and a smaller jar needs more pourings
phases.says: Pour and count. Will a smaller jar need more pourings or fewer?
phases.check: How many 400 mL mugs fill a jug that holds 2 L 800 mL? Work it out, then pour to check if you can.
phases.feels: a small jar goes back and forth many times, and a big one needs only a few
phases.hands: Give each group jars of one size and a bottle, and a table with every cell empty. One child fills the jar from a bucket and pours it into the bottle while the group counts each pouring aloud, until the bottle is full, and only then is the count written in its cell. Groups swap jars, fill every cell, and compare tables only when all of them are done.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how much does one jar hold, and how much does the bottle hold? Second rung, the phase's: is the bottle full yet? Third rung: the bottle is cut to a small one that takes only a few pourings, and the child counts them aloud before the full bottle comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: more water in a jar sounds like more of everything, and the count is heard as another way of saying how much.
wrong.move: predicts that the larger jar will need more pourings to fill the bottle, because it holds more.
wrong.screen: both jars are poured into the same bottle one after the other, each pouring a sky blue mark on the counter, and each count drops into its cell only when the bottle is full. The larger jar's cell holds the smaller count. The child's prediction stays written beside the table, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the table's empty cells look like questions to be answered, and a guess is quicker than pouring.
wrong.move: writes a count in a cell before pouring, copying it from another group or guessing it.
wrong.screen: the cell stays shut and the child's number waits beside it, written small. The jar is dipped and poured, each pouring marked on the counter, and when the bottle reaches its neck line the counted marks drop into the cell. Both numbers stay drawn, the child's beside the poured one.

wrong.why: each tip of the mug felt like one pouring, and the last one looked the same as the others.
wrong.move: counts a mug of four hundred millilitres as filling a jug of one litre five hundred millilitres in four pourings, when the fourth pouring stops with water still in the mug.
wrong.screen: three full pourings bring the jug to one thousand two hundred millilitres, and the fourth stops at the neck line with a hundred millilitres still drawn in the mug. The counter marks that pouring as part of a mug, and the mug is seen not to go into the jug exactly. The child's four stays beside the counter.

phases.screen: the jar shelf, an empty bottle, and the results table with every cell blank
phases.soWhat: When a jar goes into a bottle exactly, the pourings say how many of that jar fill it. For the same bottle, a smaller jar then needs more pourings.
phases.concept: How many small jars fill a bottle

writeup.delight: The third phase, when the story has run to its end and the run control is pressed again. The tank plays the story backwards, each amount used pouring back in and each amount added lifting out, line by line up the story card, and the level climbs back to exactly the starting mark and stops there. The answer the child wrote stays on the card through it all. It can be run forwards and back as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the frame is set to litres and millilitres, with two capacities waiting beside it, one with a two-digit number of millilitres. On the second a sum stands in the frame whose millilitres will pass a thousand, with a take-away under it whose millilitres on top are too few. On the third the tank stands full to its starting mark with the story card beside it, and the answer card's blank reads water left in the tank. On the fourth the jar shelf stands beside an empty bottle, and every cell of the results table is blank. The running count at the top left holds the columns worked or the story's lines run against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the short card, or the millilitres column, or the story card, or the smallest jar, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many boxes the millilitres take. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any capacities added or taken away in the frame under any unit pair, the tank run in any order, and any jar poured into either bottle. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first: three places for millilitres, carrying and borrowing a litre, answering in the question's words, and counting the pourings that fill a container.
voiceLines: A tank, a frame and a shelf of jars. How many boxes do the millilitres take?
The millilitres column has three boxes. How is a two-digit number of millilitres written?
More than a thousand here, too few there. Carry a litre, or break one?
What does the question ask for? Say the answer in those words.
Pour and count. Will a smaller jar need more pourings or fewer?
A new question. Say what it asks for before you work.
Free play. Any capacities in the frame, the tank in any order, and any jar into either bottle.
Read the question once more, and work the millilitres first.
Every litre carried or broken as a thousand, every answer in the question's words, and every count poured before it was written.

observations.why: A thousand joins each of those pairs, just as it joins litres and millilitres.
observations.soWhat: Beside litres the millilitres take three places, as metres do beside kilometres and grams beside kilograms.
observations.observe: Flipping the unit switch changed the headings to kilometres and metres and to kilograms and grams, and the three boxes stayed.

observations.why: A litre is a thousand millilitres, whichever way the work is going.
observations.soWhat: Each full thousand millilitres is carried as one litre, and to borrow, one litre is broken into a thousand millilitres.
observations.observe: A full thousand millilitres rose as one litre in the sum, and a broken litre poured in as a thousand in the take-away.

observations.why: The question asked how much was left at the end, after every line of the story.
observations.soWhat: Work a story's steps in the order it gives, and answer in the question's own words: what is left, not just a difference.
observations.observe: The tank settled at its last level, and the answer card took the amount only with the words water left in the tank.

observations.why: Each jar went into the bottle exactly. So its count is how many of that jar make the bottle, and a smaller jar takes more.
observations.soWhat: When a jar goes into a bottle exactly, the pourings say how many of that jar fill it. For the same bottle, a smaller jar then needs more pourings.
observations.observe: Each jar's count appeared only when its bottle was full, and the smaller jar's count was the larger.

source_tool.description: A litres and millilitres column frame fills the middle of the stage, the millilitres column fixed at three boxes and a joining sign over it reading a thousand. A unit switch can relabel the frame for kilometres and metres or kilograms and grams, and the work is the same. Adding runs the millilitres first, each full thousand carried as one litre; taking away breaks one litre into a thousand millilitres when the millilitres on top are too few or none. A tank at the left shows its water level falling and rising as amounts are used and added in the order a story gives, and an answer card beside it has a blank shaped by the question, how much is left, which is more and by how much, or the total, and will not take a bare number. At the right a jar shelf holds jars of one hundred, two hundred, two hundred and fifty and five hundred millilitres, with a one litre and a two litre bottle beside it. A jar is filled from a bucket and poured into a bottle again and again, each pouring counted, until the bottle is full, and a results table below fills a cell only when its pouring is done. No count appears anywhere on the stage before it is poured. A sort rail lines up measures written in one unit from largest to smallest.
source_tool.art_direction: A tank, a frame and jars / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a workbench with a tray of everyday things, a fifteen centimetre ruler, a ladder of units, a column frame with a unit switch, a pan balance with iron weights, a tap, jugs, glasses, jars, bottles and a tank.

A ruler is drawn as the page draws it: a long tick at every centimetre and a short one at every half, the numerals one to fifteen, and a first tick carrying the unit name and no numeral. That first tick is the zero mark and lights as one.
Every measure is written with its unit named, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, as in 4 km 66 m. A measure in two units is never written as a decimal on any stage.

The smaller unit's places are fixed boxes: three beside kilometres, kilograms and litres, two beside metres and one beside centimetres. A zero filling one of those boxes is drawn at full size and weight and is never dimmed or dropped.

A number that joins two units is shown beside them wherever the child works with them: ten between millimetres and centimetres, a hundred between centimetres and metres, and a thousand between metres and kilometres, grams and kilograms, and millilitres and litres. Weight and capacity carry one number only, a thousand.
What is left after dividing is drawn in its own slot in the smaller unit, at full strength, and it is never folded into the quotient.

A larger unit broken to borrow is drawn as exactly the joining number of smaller pieces: ten pieces for a centimetre, a hundred for a metre, and a thousand for a kilometre, a kilogram or a litre, the thousand drawn as ten bars of a hundred.
No count, reading or result is shown before the child makes it. A jar count appears only once the pouring is done, and a reading only once the object is laid.
Every word on the stage says weight, the vocabulary box's word, for how heavy a thing is.
A container whose capacity is shown is drawn full to its brim.
Two measures being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a bar, a weight or a liquid the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that pads the smaller unit's places, as in zero seven five, is grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded, because it is holding a place. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape and the mark where a reading is taken are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket and table rule, is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because each unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, and a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the question once more, and work the millilitres first.
voice.onNext: A new question. Say what it asks for before you work.
voice.opening: A tank, a frame and a shelf of jars. How many boxes do the millilitres take?
voice.onFinish: Every litre carried or broken as a thousand, every answer in the question's words, and every count poured before it was written.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any capacities in the frame, the tank in any order, and any jar into either bottle.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: How many small jars fill a bottle

placement.where: After groups have filled a one litre and a two litre bottle with jars of different sizes and written their counts in a table before comparing tables. The tool is what keeps each count off the stage until it is poured, and will not take a bare number where the question asks what is left.

answer_key.rule: Beside litres, millilitres take three places, as metres do beside kilometres and grams beside kilograms. Add or take away the millilitres first. Each full thousand millilitres is carried as one litre. When the millilitres on top are too few, one litre is broken into a thousand millilitres and the litres on top go down by one. An answer says what the question asks: how much is left, which is more and by how much, or the total, in the units the question uses. When a story uses and adds amounts in turn, work them in the order it gives. When a jar's capacity goes exactly into a bottle's, the pourings needed are the number of jars that make the bottle's capacity. For the same bottle, a smaller jar needs more pourings. Lengths, weights and capacities in two units are added and taken away the same way, each pair with its own joining number.
answer_key.wrong: The frame is redrawn a column at a time with the thousand lit. Or the tank runs the story again step by step, or the jar is poured again with each pouring counted aloud. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Beside litres, millilitres take three places, so 40 mL is written 040.
Add the litres: 23 and 15 make 38. The sum is 38 L 725 mL.
items.question: Add 23 L 40 mL and 15 L 685 mL in columns.
items.checkpoint: Beside litres, millilitres take three places, just like grams and metres.
items.misconception: Writing 40 mL under the hundreds and tens of 685, which turns it into 400 mL.

steps: 1265 mL is 1 L 265 mL, so write 265 and carry 1 L.
Add the litres with the carry: 36 and 48 and 1 make 85. The sum is 85 L 265 mL.
items.question: Add 36 L 575 mL and 48 L 690 mL.
items.checkpoint: Each full thousand millilitres is carried as one litre; taking away, one litre is broken into a thousand millilitres.
items.misconception: Writing 1265 in the millilitres column, which leaves the column holding more than a litre.

steps: Write 50 L as 50 L 000 mL. There are no millilitres on top, so break one litre into a thousand: 49 L 1000 mL.
The question asks what is left, so the answer says it: 17 L 350 mL of water is left in the tank.
items.answer: 17 L 350 mL of water is left in the tank
items.question: A tank holds 50 L of water. 32 L 650 mL of it is used. How much water is left in the tank?
items.checkpoint: Answer in the words of the question: what is left, not just a difference.
items.misconception: Ending on the difference is 17 L 350 mL without saying what it is, or taking 0 from 650 the wrong way round and getting 18 L 650 mL.

steps: Write the jug's capacity in millilitres: 2 L 400 mL is 2400 mL.
That is 8 pourings, so 8 glasses fill the jug. Check: 8 times 300 is 2400.
items.question: How many 300 mL glasses fill a jug that holds 2 L 400 mL?
items.checkpoint: For the same container, a smaller glass or jar needs more pourings.
items.misconception: Thinking a bigger glass needs more pourings because it holds more, or counting the 2 L as 2 glasses.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How is 8 mL written in the millilitres column beside litres?
19 L 65 mL is written in columns. What goes in the millilitres column?
Add 14 L 380 mL, 26 L 745 mL and 9 L 90 mL.
items.final_answer: 50 L 215 mL. The millilitres make 1215, so write 215 and carry 1 L

items.question: One cow gives 12 L 750 mL of milk and another gives 14 L 380 mL. Which cow gives more milk, and how much more?
items.final_answer: The second cow gives more, by 1 L 630 mL. Break one litre: 13 L 1380 mL less 12 L 750 mL

items.question: A jar holds 5 L of juice. 2 L 640 mL of it is poured out. How much juice is left in the jar?
items.final_answer: 2 L 360 mL of juice is left in the jar

items.question: A water tank has 60 L. First 34 L 500 mL is used, then 20 L is added, then 27 L 750 mL is used. How much water is left in the tank?
items.final_answer: 17 L 750 mL of water is left. 60 L less 34 L 500 mL is 25 L 500 mL, 20 L more makes 45 L 500 mL, and taking 27 L 750 mL leaves 17 L 750 mL

items.question: How many 150 mL cups fill a bottle that holds 1 L 200 mL?
items.final_answer: 8 cups, because 8 times 150 mL is 1200 mL

items.question: A 400 mL mug and a 200 mL glass are each used to fill a jug of 3 L 200 mL. How many pourings does each need, and which needs more?
items.final_answer: The mug needs 8 and the glass needs 16, so the smaller glass needs more pourings

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Before the tool is opened, have groups fill a one litre and a two litre bottle with jars of different sizes. Each group writes its counts in a table before anyone compares. The page prints its results for the one litre bottle before anyone pours, and its picture draws exactly those jars, so keep the table covered and let the counts be found. Example 17 asks how much water is left in the container and ends by calling its answer the difference; say instead how much is left. Exercise 11.6 asks who sold more and how much more, which is two answers. The Critical Thinking box uses petrol, buys more and uses again; work it in the order given, because using the second amount before buying would take the tank below empty. The same column work runs for lengths and weights, each pair with its own joining number. The vocabulary box lists six words for flashcards: metre, kilogram, litre, length, weight and capacity; the metre, the kilogram and the litre are the standard units of the other three. The self-assessment has three statements: listing units, changing them, and adding and taking away. Apply Your Skills turns a table of throws into centimetres and puts each event in descending order, largest first, which the sort rail does once each throw is in centimetres. Its three further questions ask for facts the chapter does not give, and this plan does not answer them.
generation_prompt: Build a column and pouring tool for capacities on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A two-column frame headed L and mL fills the middle of the working area, the mL column fixed at exactly three digit boxes, with a joining sign over the frame reading a thousand; a unit switch relabels the headings km and m, or kg and g, and the boxes stay three. Adding works the mL column first, each full thousand carried as one litre chip; taking away breaks one litre chip into a thousand millilitres, drawn as ten bars of a hundred, when the millilitres on top are fewer than those below or read 000. At the left a tank shows a pale blue water level that falls and rises step by step as a story card uses and adds amounts in its own order, and an answer card beside it offers a blank shaped by the question, how much is left, which is more and by how much, or the total, and will not accept a bare number. At the right a jar shelf holds jars of 100, 200, 250 and 500 mL with a one litre and a two litre bottle; a jar is filled from a bucket and poured into a bottle again and again, each pouring counted in sky blue, until the bottle is full, and only then does its count drop into a cell of the results table below. Every cell starts empty and no count is shown anywhere before it is poured. A sort rail lines up measures written in one unit from largest to smallest. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fill all three millilitres boxes. Work the millilitres first. Carry or break a litre as a thousand. Answer in the question's words. Pour and count before you write.
